strengths: Cell-MNN is a conceptually interesting adaptation of mechanistic neural networks to snapshot single-cell data, combining a state-conditioned linear operator, an analytic matrix-exponential decoder, and distribution matching without dataset-wide optimal-transport preprocessing.

The interpolation results are promising: the method obtains the best average EMD across three real datasets and includes several recent, relevant baselines, a simple OT-interpolation reference, multiple seeds, and held-out-time evaluation.

The paper examines useful practical dimensions beyond standard interpolation, including joint training across datasets, scaling to larger sample counts, computational cost, and biological interpretation.

The presentation is generally clear, with a helpful problem formulation, an explicit loss, hyperparameter and compute details, limitations and ethics discussions, and an appendix containing numerical results and the factorization proposition.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic interpretation is not technically justified. Because A(z,t) is state-dependent, the Jacobian of the learned velocity A(z,t)z contains an additional derivative-of-A term; consequently, V_PCA A V_PCA^T is not generally the local gene-to-gene influence matrix of the learned nonlinear dynamics. Moreover, decompositions f(z,t)=A(z,t)z are highly non-unique, so predictive supervision need not identify the entries of A. These issues substantially undermine the claim of discovering explicit gene-regulatory interactions.

The TRRUST experiment is too weak to repair this identifiability problem. It evaluates only the activation/repression sign of already known edges for six model-selected source genes, with as few as ten evaluated interactions, rather than recovering edges among all genes. It provides no comparison with established GRN-inference methods, no evaluation of false-positive edges, and no assessment using perturbational or held-out biological data. The reported zero-eigenvalue bias also improves only some genes and has large variance, despite being described as significantly beneficial.

Trajectory dynamics are fundamentally non-identifiable from snapshot marginals, yet the experiments establish distributional interpolation rather than recovery of the true dynamics. Synthetic systems with known vector fields or regulatory networks, perturbation data, and stability tests across seeds or equivalent predictive solutions are needed to demonstrate that the learned operators correspond to genuine mechanisms.

The predictive evidence is narrower than the claims suggest. Results cover only three datasets in a five-dimensional PCA space; uncertainty in the main table is reported over held-out time points rather than clearly aggregating the three training seeds; statistical significance is not assessed; and important ablations of the operator parameterization, kinetic and invertibility regularizers, latent dimension, and direct velocity or unconstrained-matrix alternatives are absent.

The scalability study inflates existing datasets by resampling and adding Gaussian noise, evaluates with the same MMD family used for training, and mainly demonstrates expected OOM behavior of full-dataset Sinkhorn. It lacks runtime and peak-memory curves or scaling across multiple sample sizes, while the competitive minibatch-OT baseline substantially weakens the broad scalability claim.

The amortization experiment jointly fits only two datasets using a dataset identifier and separate PCA coordinate systems. It shows parameter sharing, but neither transfer to an unseen dataset nor a clear improvement over separately trained Cell-MNN models; thus the foundation-model and transfer-learning motivation is not demonstrated.

Several implementation and evaluation details remain unclear, including what data are used for frequent validation and early stopping when the target time point is held out, how grid-search hyperparameters are selected without test-time leakage, and the exact multi-step sampling procedure for the marginal loss. The determinant-based penalty 1/(det(P)+epsilon) also does not guarantee invertibility and can behave pathologically for negative determinants.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem at the intersection of machine learning and single-cell biology: jointly predicting population dynamics and extracting potentially interpretable structure.
Cell-MNN is conceptually simple and computationally attractive. Its closed-form latent transition avoids numerical ODE integration and dataset-wide optimal-transport preprocessing.
The interpolation results are promising: the method obtains the best reported average EMD across three datasets and performs particularly well on EB and Multi.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes hyperparameters, hardware, multiple seeds, an ethics statement, and experiments covering interpolation, amortization, scalability, and biological interpretation.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic-interpretability claim is not technically justified. Training constrains the action of A(z,t) on observed states, but does not uniquely identify the full matrix. Many operators can induce the same transitions, so individual entries of V_PCA A V_PCA^T cannot automatically be interpreted as identifiable gene-regulatory effects. The proposition establishing that f(z,t)=A(z,t)z exists does not address this non-identifiability.

The proposed transition freezes A at the initial operating point and applies exp(A Δt). This is not generally the solution of the stated nonlinear, time-dependent ODE z'=A(z,t)z, whose operator should change along the trajectory. No semigroup, rollout-consistency, or local-approximation analysis is provided, weakening the claim that the model learns explicit governing dynamics rather than a structured conditional transition map.

The TRRUST experiment does not demonstrate gene-interaction discovery. It evaluates only activation-versus-repression signs for already-known TRRUST edges, after selecting six source genes based on model activity and database overlap. It neither predicts whether an edge exists nor compares against established GRN-inference methods, simple correlation/PCA controls, or class-prior baselines. Averaging across all cells also discards the context specificity emphasized by the paper.

Projecting a five-dimensional PCA operator back to thousands of genes produces a dense, rank-at-most-five matrix strongly determined by PCA loadings. The paper does not establish that its entries correspond to causal or direct biological regulation, study sensitivity to PCA dimension or rotation, or assess stability of recovered interactions across folds and preprocessing choices.

The determinant regularizer 1/(det(P)+epsilon) does not reliably enforce invertibility: it is scale-sensitive, can be driven down by rescaling eigenvectors without changing A, and becomes singular or potentially unbounded near det(P)=-epsilon. Numerical conditioning of P and P^{-1} is not reported.

The empirical evidence is insufficient for several broader claims. The scalability study uses duplicated observations with synthetic Gaussian noise, changes the evaluation metric to the same MMD family used for training, and reports OOM on one 11-GB GPU rather than runtime/memory scaling curves. The amortization experiment uses only two datasets with dataset identifiers and separate PCA embeddings, and tests neither transfer nor generalization to an unseen dataset.

Ablations are very limited. There is no comparison to a capacity-matched direct transition network, a standard Neural ODE trained with the same objective, or Action Matching; nor are the matrix-exponential parameterization, kinetic penalty, MMD objective, and operator conditioning individually assessed. Statistical reporting is also unclear because standard deviations are described as being over held-out time points despite experiments using three seeds, and the validation split used for early stopping and hyperparameter search is not specified.

strengths: Cell-MNN presents a clear and useful modeling idea: predict a state-conditioned linear latent ODE, use its matrix exponential for analytic propagation, and train directly against population marginals without dataset-wide optimal-transport preprocessing.
The interpolation results are encouraging. Across three established single-cell datasets, Cell-MNN obtains the best reported average EMD and is particularly strong on EB and Multi.

The paper evaluates several practically relevant dimensions beyond standard interpolation, including joint training across datasets, behavior on synthetically enlarged datasets, and biological interpretation.
The presentation is generally clear, with a helpful architecture description, explicit complexity discussion, detailed hyperparameters, three-seed experiments, and an appropriate ethics statement.
The computational profile is attractive: training uses modest hardware, avoids numerical ODE integration, and admits an efficient analytic decoder in the low-dimensional latent space.
weaknesses: The central gene-regulatory interpretation is not sufficiently justified. From V^T x-dot = A V^T x, the paper incorrectly claims the equivalence x-dot = V A V^T x; only the projection V V^T x-dot is determined unless the entire state and its derivative lie in the five-dimensional PCA subspace. Consequently, the reported gene-space operator is a rank-at-most-five reconstruction rather than an identified full gene-regulatory mechanism.

The learned operator is highly non-identifiable. Supervision primarily constrains the action of A(z,t) on the current latent state, while many matrices can produce the same local velocity or finite-step prediction. Proposition 1 establishes existence, not uniqueness, and no structural constraint or recovery analysis shows that individual matrix entries correspond to causal gene interactions.

The invertibility regularizer 1/(det(P)+epsilon) is technically problematic as written. It neither controls the condition number nor reliably guarantees invertibility, is invariantly exploitable by rescaling eigenvectors, and can become unbounded below when the determinant approaches -epsilon. This raises both soundness and reproducibility concerns.

The biological evaluation is narrow and selection-sensitive: it covers only six highly studied source genes selected using both model activity and TRRUST overlap, tests only activation versus repression on already-known edges, and includes no comparison with established GRN-inference methods or matched null models. It therefore does not demonstrate recovery of interaction existence or novel regulatory structure.

The scalability evidence uses duplicated observations with added Gaussian noise, changes the evaluation metric from EMD to the same MMD family used for training, and reports OOM outcomes on one 11-GB GPU rather than runtime and memory curves over dataset sizes. This supports feasibility but not a broad scalability advantage.

The amortization study jointly trains on only two datasets, supplies a dataset identifier, and uses unrelated dataset-specific PCA coordinate systems. It shows parameter sharing but provides little evidence of beneficial transfer or generalization to unseen datasets.

Because A is frozen at the initial operating point during each finite-step matrix-exponential prediction, the model is not guaranteed to define compositionally consistent trajectories. No semigroup-consistency, long-horizon, or relinearization analysis is provided.

Baseline values are partly imported from prior work, uncertainty is reported over held-out time points rather than consistently over random seeds, and statistical significance is not assessed. No code or repository is identified, limiting full reproducibility.
